title: MCB trips under load
summary: The breaker holds at low demand but trips when kettles, heaters, or multiple appliances run together, suggesting thermal overcurrent stress rather than an instant short.
description: Learners should distinguish nuisance load stacking from wiring defects by observing when tripping starts and whether one circuit is repeatedly involved.
dangerNotes: Repeated resetting can overheat conductors and accessories. Do not bypass protection or fit a larger breaker.
commonSymptoms: Trips after 5–20 minutes of heavy use
More likely in evenings when multiple loads run
One room/circuit affected while others stay live
No trip when high-power appliances are unplugged
likelyCauses: Sustained overload on a radial or spur
Undersized cable section on altered branch
safeChecks: List all high-watt appliances running together
Unplug non-essential loads and retry once
Note exact breaker label and rating
Look for discolouration at plugs/sockets externally
escalationRules: Escalate if breaker trips with minimal load
Escalate immediately if smell/heat is present
Escalate if breaker rating/label is unclear
Escalate when tripping has increased in frequency
escalationGuidance: Escalate using the listed escalation rules and stop at safety boundaries.
electricianTestsNext: Verify design current versus protective device rating
Measure load current under controlled demand
educationalExplanation: Overcurrent stress can damage insulation over time and become a fire risk if ignored.

title: RCD trips immediately
summary: The RCD drops out as soon as it is reset or as soon as a circuit is energized, indicating leakage or a neutral-earth fault path.
description: This pattern points to imbalance current and requires careful isolation logic to separate appliance leakage from fixed-wiring problems.
dangerNotes: Persistent earth leakage can indicate damaged insulation or exposed conductive paths.
commonSymptoms: Trips when a single circuit is enabled
Reset works only after unplugging appliances
safeChecks: Unplug portable appliances before one reset attempt
Identify if one breaker consistently correlates
Check for outdoor moisture signs
Record weather/time correlation
escalationRules: Escalate if RCD trips with all loads unplugged
Escalate if any shock/tingle was reported
Escalate if outdoor equipment is water affected
Escalate if board labeling is ambiguous
escalationGuidance: Escalate using the listed escalation rules and stop at safety boundaries.
electricianTestsNext: Dead testing to locate N-E fault
Sequential circuit reconnection under controlled test
educationalExplanation: RCD operation is a life-safety warning and should be treated as evidence of leakage risk, not inconvenience.

title: RCBO trips on one circuit
summary: A single RCBO repeatedly trips, narrowing the issue to one final circuit and allowing focused diagnosis.
description: Because RCBOs protect both overcurrent and leakage, symptom timing is key to infer whether load, short, or insulation issues dominate.
dangerNotes: Repeated re-energization can worsen thermal or insulation damage.
commonSymptoms: Trip after some minutes under load
Circuit stable when one accessory avoided
safeChecks: Log exact trigger moment
Unplug all items on that circuit
Observe one accessory at a time without dismantling
Check for visible damage at affected outlet
escalationRules: Escalate if tripping resumes with nothing plugged in
Escalate for heat, arcing sounds, or burning smell
Escalate if circuit serves critical equipment
Escalate if board schedule is missing
escalationGuidance: Escalate using the listed escalation rules and stop at safety boundaries.
educationalExplanation: Fast circuit isolation helps prevent broad outages and identifies dangerous points before failure spreads.

title: Some sockets dead, others live
summary: Part of a socket circuit remains energized while other points are dead, often signaling ring discontinuity or localized disconnection.
description: Learners should map which outlets are dead/live to understand likely circuit topology issues.
dangerNotes: Broken ring conditions can overload one leg and create hidden overheating.
commonSymptoms: Dead outlets correspond to recent decorating area
One twin outlet half behaves inconsistently
safeChecks: Map live/dead outlets on paper
Avoid high-load use on remaining live points
Check for visible damage to faceplates only
Ask if any recent drilling occurred
escalationRules: Escalate if multiple outlets heat under moderate load
Escalate if dead/live pattern changes quickly
Escalate when cable damage is suspected
Escalate if ring final integrity is uncertain
escalationGuidance: Escalate using the listed escalation rules and stop at safety boundaries.
educationalExplanation: Partial failures can hide dangerous overload paths that are not obvious to occupants.

title: Whole socket circuit dead
summary: All sockets on one circuit are unavailable, pointing to protective device operation, supply interruption, or a major open-circuit fault.
description: The learner focus is to identify scope and triggering event without opening accessories.
dangerNotes: Do not repeatedly force resets; underlying faults can be severe.
commonSymptoms: Entire room group of sockets off
No response from plug-in tester on affected points
safeChecks: Confirm exactly which circuits are off
Check board handle positions visually
Unplug all loads before one reset attempt
Record which event preceded outage
escalationRules: Escalate if breaker immediately retrips
Escalate if outage follows burning smell
Escalate if board access is unsafe
Escalate where vulnerable occupants rely on equipment
escalationGuidance: Escalate using the listed escalation rules and stop at safety boundaries.
educationalExplanation: Circuit-wide outages can indicate serious single-point failures with safety implications.

title: Lights not working on one floor
summary: A section of lighting is lost while other lighting remains, suggesting local feed/switch-line/neutral issues.
description: Structured questioning should separate lamp failure, switch wiring issues, and protective-device operation.
dangerNotes: Ceiling void wiring faults can escalate if repeatedly switched under fault conditions.
commonSymptoms: All lamps on one level out
Switches feel normal but no light output
safeChecks: Confirm affected area boundaries
Try known-good lamp where user-replaceable
Check if any breaker/RCBO is down
Note if failure followed DIY decoration
escalationRules: Escalate if combined with tripping
Escalate if fittings show heat marks
Escalate if failure is intermittent and spreading
Escalate if ladder/height work would be needed
escalationGuidance: Escalate using the listed escalation rules and stop at safety boundaries.
electricianTestsNext: Continuity of switched line and neutral
educationalExplanation: Lighting faults can indicate hidden connection problems that may overheat before complete failure.

title: Lights flicker or dim
summary: Brightness fluctuates, especially when appliances start, which may indicate voltage drop, loose connections, or shared neutral issues.
description: Observing patterns by time and concurrent loads helps identify if variation is local, circuit-level, or supply-related.
dangerNotes: Flicker plus heat or buzzing can indicate arcing risk.
safeChecks: Log which loads trigger dimming
Observe if all rooms or one room affected
Listen for buzzing without touching internals
Check visible lamp compatibility labels
escalationRules: Escalate if flicker accompanies burning smell
Escalate if multiple circuits flicker together
Escalate if switches/sockets feel warm
Escalate if vulnerable users are impacted
escalationGuidance: Escalate using the listed escalation rules and stop at safety boundaries.
electricianTestsNext: Measure voltage drop under controlled load
educationalExplanation: Voltage instability can be early evidence of poor connections that later fail dangerously.

title: Socket or switch feels hot / shows burn marks
summary: Accessory surface heat, discoloration, or burn marks indicate high-resistance contact or overloading and require immediate stop-use behavior.
description: This is a safety-first case: observation only, no dismantling, with rapid escalation.
dangerNotes: Potential active arcing/fire hazard. Treat as urgent.
commonSymptoms: Brown marks near terminals or plug pins
likelyCauses: Damaged plug pins causing poor contact
safeChecks: Stop using affected point
Unplug loads if safe
Compare nearby accessories for abnormal heat
Photograph visible damage for electrician
escalationRules: Immediate escalation for any burn marks
Immediate escalation for smell or smoke
Escalate if child-accessible location
Escalate if multiple points are heating
escalationGuidance: Escalate using the listed escalation rules and stop at safety boundaries.
educationalExplanation: Thermal damage can progress to ignition quickly, even if power seems to return.

title: Appliance causes trip when plugged in

description: Cross-checking on another known-good socket helps isolate appliance versus fixed wiring contribution.
dangerNotes: Do not continue using a suspect appliance that trips protection.
commonSymptoms: Trip occurs with one specific appliance
Trip timing differs between plug-in and switch-on
Visible flex wear near entry gland

Try a different low-risk appliance in same socket
Inspect plug/flex externally
Record trip device type and timing

Escalate if trip persists with appliance unplugged

Observe for heat or buzzing at switches
Avoid removing faceplates

escalationGuidance: Escalate using the listed escalation rules and stop at safety boundaries.

title: Low insulation resistance suspected
summary: Symptoms suggest insulation breakdown such as damp-related leakage, aged cable deterioration, or damaged accessories.
description: This is inference-only in learner mode: confirmation requires qualified dead testing with calibrated instruments.
dangerNotes: Degraded insulation can permit leakage current and indirect contact risk.
commonSymptoms: Older circuit with recurring nuisance trips
safeChecks: Correlate faults with humidity/weather
Identify affected zones (kitchen/outdoors/loft)
Avoid repeated reset attempts
Collect history of prior similar incidents
escalationRules: Escalate if trips persist with all appliances unplugged

educationalExplanation: Insulation weakness can worsen rapidly and may not be visible until dangerous failure occurs.

title: Loose connection / overheating suspected
summary: Symptoms suggest a high-resistance joint where current flow causes localized heating, voltage drop, and intermittent operation.
description: Observation should prioritize identifying where symptoms concentrate and enforcing stop-use if heat is evident.
dangerNotes: High-resistance joints can arc and ignite surrounding materials.
commonSymptoms: Intermittent power loss on one point
Heat at accessory or consumer unit front
safeChecks: Reduce load on suspect branch
Observe whether issue tracks one accessory
Record timing with heavy demand
Check for discoloration externally

Immediate escalation for repeated crackling
Escalate if issue affects board area
Escalate if outages are worsening

Keep affected circuits de-energized if practical

title: Broken ring final suspected
